description: Junior AI Engineer and pre-master student at asu
summary:
Tira Nova is a search engine and dashboard that ranks places on Earth by how closely they resemble a chosen Mars landing site or rover route. It lets mission teams pick rehearsal sites systematically instead of reusing the same few famous deserts.
We scan the whole planet. 41,034 Earth windows and 47,354 Mars windows (about 50.9 km across) are compared on terrain using NASA SRTM and MOLA elevation, which gives 228,721 candidate rows. We then add mineral evidence: CRISM shows which minerals are detected at five Mars sites (20 site-mineral targets), and EMIT shows whether a candidate Earth window has the same minerals. Terrain and minerals combine into one score, served by a read-only API and a web dashboard.
Every result carries its distance, its evidence and its warnings. Only 55 Earth windows have EMIT data so far, the CRISM detection rule is our own heuristic, and similarity is not equivalence. Surface-texture and thermal comparisons are included as labelled exploratory demos and are not part of the ranking.
It matters because a poor analog teaches a mission team the wrong lessons before launch.
details:
What it does. A user chooses a Mars site (Jezero, Gale, Gale Bradbury, Meridiani, Oxia Planum, Zhurong or InSight) and a mission type (landing site, rover mobility or overall terrain). Tira Nova returns a ranked list of Earth windows, each with a score, a terrain distance, the mineral evidence and warning flags. The dashboard draws the results on a map, in English and Arabic.

How it works.

  1. Terrain scan. The engine cuts Earth (SRTM, about 450 m per pixel) and Mars (MOLA, 463 m) into 50.9 km windows and computes a distance between every Mars window and every eligible Earth window. A smaller distance means closer terrain. Each result is flagged non_discriminating when more than 10% of the eligible Earth windows are inside the good distance, because then the rank barely separates candidates.
  2. Mars minerals (CRISM). From 21 orbital observations we detect minerals per site with a relative threshold on CRISM spectral parameters, giving 20 site-mineral targets. Minerals that share the same spectral parameters are grouped into one independent signal.
  3. Earth minerals (EMIT). EMIT mineral abundance at 480 m shows whether a candidate Earth window contains the same signals.
  4. Combined score. score = 0.5 × (1 − terrain distance ratio) + 0.5 × (signals found / signals needed). The final file has 312 rows, 40 of them mineral-ranked.
  5. Delivery. A read-only FastAPI service serves the results as JSON, including the limits text and caution flags for every row.

Results. Jezero's landing-site query returns a window in the Atacama Desert first, which agrees with the known analog. Its rover query returns a window in Namibia that shows both mineral signals but has weakly discriminating terrain. We show that flag next to the result.

Exploratory layers (not in the ranking). Surface texture (CTX against HLS) was perturbation-unstable, so we report no winner. A thermal run compares the day–night temperature range from THEMIS and MODIS Aqua for two Mars sites and four Earth windows; the two quantities are not equal, so only ranks are comparable.

Benefits. The search is repeatable, covers whole continents and is auditable: each recommendation shows the numbers behind it. Mission planners, rover and instrument teams, field geologists and educators can use it.

What we hope to achieve. Run EMIT on the 127 top terrain and known-analog windows, field-check the top Egyptian and Namibian windows, then extend the same engine to Artemis candidate sites on the Moon.

Honest limits. Terrain is regional, not rover-scale. EMIT covers only 55 Earth windows, so the mineral ranking covers that subset. 29 of the 40 ranked rows have weakly discriminating terrain. CRISM covers 5 to 13% of each window and its detection rule is a heuristic. Several thresholds are provisional project choices.

Tools. Python and Jupyter or Colab, pandas, numpy, rasterio, scikit-image, earthaccess, FastAPI and uvicorn. Dashboard front end: next.js
